title: Box Office Shock: ‘Other Mommy’ Rakes $12.6M Opening Day, ‘The Social Reckoning’ Opens at $2.15M
body:
The horror‑thriller “Other Mommy” roared into theaters on Friday, pulling in an impressive $12.6 million on its opening day and seizing the number‑one spot at the domestic box office. Its supernatural, psychological chill was matched only by the modest debut of the documentary “The Social Reckoning,” which earned $2.15 million on the same day. The figures underscore a broader trend: horror continues to dominate the 2026 cinema landscape, a momentum that shows no signs of waning as Halloween approaches.

“Other Mommy,” directed by rising auteur Maya Lin, taps into contemporary anxieties about motherhood and identity, weaving a narrative that blends eerie folklore with modern family drama. The film’s marketing campaign, which leaned heavily on social‑media teasers and viral “creepypasta” style clips, appears to have paid off, resonating with both genre aficionados and casual moviegoers. Its $12.6 million opening not only eclipses the $9.4 million debut of the sci‑fi thriller “Quantum Rift” last week, but also places it among the top‑grossing horror openings of the year, trailing only the $15.2 million launch of “Obsession” and the $13.8 million debut of “Backrooms.”

The success of “Other Mommy” arrives on the heels of a string of strong horror releases that have collectively reshaped the box‑office calendar. Earlier this spring, “Resident Evil: Extinction” delivered $11.3 million on its first day, while “The Haunting of Hillcrest” logged $10.1 million in its opening weekend. Analysts attribute this surge to a confluence of factors: a renewed appetite for communal, adrenaline‑driven experiences after a year of streaming fatigue, and studios’ willingness to invest in mid‑budget genre films that promise high returns relative to their production costs.

Conversely, “The Social Reckoning,” a documentary examining the influence of algorithmic feeds on public discourse, struggled to find an audience beyond niche interest groups. Its $2.15 million opening reflects the challenges faced by non‑fiction fare in a market saturated with high‑concept horror and blockbuster franchises. While the film has been praised for its investigative depth and timely subject matter, its modest earnings highlight the difficulty of drawing mass audiences to socially‑charged content without the draw of star power or genre hooks.

Industry observers note that the horror genre’s dominance is not merely a fleeting fad but part of a strategic shift in studio programming. With production budgets for horror typically ranging from $10 million to $30 million, studios can achieve profitable returns even with moderate attendance. Moreover, horror’s universal themes—fear, survival, the unknown—translate well across international markets, bolstering global box‑office prospects. The upcoming releases of “The Witching Hour” and “Nightmare Manor” are already generating buzz, suggesting that the genre’s momentum will likely sustain through the holiday season.

Looking ahead, the sustained box‑office strength of horror could influence the green‑lighting of future projects, prompting studios to allocate more resources toward genre‑bending narratives that blend scares with social commentary, much like “Other Mommy.” As audiences continue to seek visceral, immersive experiences, the horror genre is poised to remain a cornerstone of theatrical revenue, especially as Halloween looms, promising another wave of spine‑tingling releases that could further redefine the cinematic landscape of 2026.
